title: Gynecoid
path: Unit I: Female Pelvic Anatomy and Obstetric Significance

headings.title: Introduction and Characteristics of the Gynecoid Pelvis
headings.content: The **gynecoid pelvis** is traditionally regarded as the classic female pelvis, ideally suited for childbearing. It occurs in about half of all women and provides the most favourable architecture for vaginal delivery. Unlike narrower pelvic types, its well-rounded contours accommodate the passage of the foetus with minimal mechanical obstruction. Midwifery students in Nigeria often encounter this pelvis type in clinical practice as the standard reference point when comparing other pelvic shapes during antenatal assessments.

headings.title: Anatomical Shape and Dimensions
headings.content:
The defining feature of the gynecoid pelvis is its rounded or slightly oval pelvic inlet. The **transverse diameter** is wide and often equals or slightly exceeds the anteroposterior diameter. Other key structural traits include:

- **Side walls**: Straight and parallel, rather than converging inward.
- **Ischial spines**: Blunt and non-prominent, creating a wide interspinous diameter.
- **Sacrum**: Wide, well-curved, and placed backward, which deepens the posterior pelvis.
- **Subpubic arch**: Wide and rounded, forming an angle of roughly 90 degrees or more.

headings.title: Pelvic Planes and Diameters
headings.content:
The internal architecture of the gynecoid pelvis is mapped through specific planes from the inlet down to the outlet. 

| Pelvic Region | Key Diameter | Average Measurement |
|---|---|---|
| **Inlet** | Anteroposterior (conjugate vera) | 11.0 cm |
| **Cavity** | Transverse dimension | 12.0 cm |
| **Outlet** | Bituberous diameter | 11.0 cm |

These generous measurements ensure that all planes—inlet, cavity, and outlet—are roomy. The mid-cavity is particularly circular, allowing smooth internal rotation of the baby's head as it navigates the birth canal.

headings.title: Obstetric Significance and Fetal Engagement
headings.content: Because the pelvic inlet is wide and rounded, the foetal head readily engages in a transverse or occipito-transverse position. Obstetricians and midwives value the gynecoid pelvis because it rarely causes cephalopelvic disproportion. The generous posterior segment provides ample space for the occiput, making occipito-posterior positions less common or easier to correct.

headings.title: Mechanism of Labour in a Gynecoid Pelvis
headings.content: The classic mechanism of labour unfolds smoothly within the gynecoid pelvis. Descent is steady, promoted by good uterine contractions. Flexion occurs easily as the head meets resistance from the pelvic floor. Internal rotation turns the occiput anteriorly toward the symphysis pubis, taking advantage of the wide subpubic arch. Extension follows as the head crowns and is born, demonstrating how well pelvic shape dictates kinematic ease.

headings.title: Clinical Identification and Pelvimetry
headings.content: Identifying a gynecoid pelvis involves clinical pelvimetry during antenatal care or early labour. Midwives assess the diagonal conjugate via vaginal examination, check the width of the subpubic arch by placing two fingers under the pubic symphysis, and palpate the ischial spines. While modern imaging like ultrasound or MRI can measure pelvimetry precisely, skilled manual examination remains a vital bedside skill across many healthcare facilities in Nigeria.
